sub.en: You have to say something difficult. Which version keeps the other person on your side?

items.q: You are opening a complaint to a colleague.
o: I’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to talk to you about something.
I am sorry for have to say this, but I need talk to you.
Sorry to must say this, but I need to talk with you about something.

items.q: You are naming the problem without naming the person yet.
o: I’m afraid there’s a problem with the noise.
I’m afraid there is a problem of the noise.
I’m afraid it has a problem with the noise.

items.q: You are asking for the change you actually want.
o: Would you mind taking the calls in your own time?
Would you mind to take the calls in your own time?
Would you mind if you take the calls in your own time?
items.why: Would you mind + -ing. It is one of the softest ways of asking for a change.

items.q: You want to make the request feel small and reasonable.
o: It would really help if you could clear up your things.
It would really help if you can clear up your things.
It would really help that you clear up your things.

items.q: You are complaining in a shop.
o: Sorry to bother you, but I’ve got a problem with this tablet.
Sorry for bother you, but I have a problem of this tablet.
Sorry to bother you, but I’m having a problem with this tablet since.

items.q: Online, somebody has made an argument you partly accept.
o: I see your point, but the figures say something different.
I see your point, but the figures are saying something different since.
I am seeing your point, but the figures say something different.
items.why: see = understand is a state verb, so the simple form is used.

items.q: You want to accept one part of what they said.
o: That’s a fair point.
That’s a fairly point.
That’s fair point.

items.q: You disagree, and you want to say so without being rude.
o: I’d have to disagree with that.
I’d have to disagree of that.
I would have disagree with that.

acts.title: Re: Should the office kitchen have a rota?
text: Re: Should the office kitchen have a rota?
Aisulu wrote that a rota would treat adults like schoolchildren.
That’s a fair point, and I’d say she’s probably right about how it would feel on day one.

I see her point, but I’d have to disagree with where it leads. In my view the problem isn’t that people are lazy; it’s that nobody knows whose turn it is. Three of us cleared the sink last week and none of us knew the others had. That can’t be a good use of anybody’s morning.
The obvious objection is that a rota will be ignored by the same people who ignore the sink now. Possibly. But a rota at least makes it visible, and visible things get done.
So: a printed list on the door, one name a day, and nobody mentions it again. It would really help if we tried it for a month before deciding.

items.r: says clearly what the writer is replying to
accepts the part of the argument that is right
gives the writer’s own view, with a concrete example
states the strongest objection and answers it

items.q: Which four words accept part of the other person’s argument?
Which four words introduce the polite disagreement? (I see … but)
Which three words open the writer’s own opinion?
Which two words make a deduction about the wasted mornings? (It … be)
Which two words name the argument against? (The obvious … )
Which five words open the proposal? (It would really help … )

acts.genre: Register · face to face or in writing
acts.title: Said across a desk, or posted for everybody?
text: Face to face you can hesitate, soften and check the other person’s reaction as you go. Half the message is in the pauses.
A post is read by people who were not in the room. It names what it is replying to, accepts what is right, and proposes something concrete.

tts: Look, I’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to talk to you about something.
Well, I’m afraid there’s a problem with noise.
Yes. There are a lot of us in this office trying to work, and it’s a bit noisy at times.
Yeah, actually you’re right. It is noisy sometimes, isn’t it?
No — what I mean is, you’re a bit noisy at times. On the phone.
Well, I did have one long call today. Sorry about that.
To be honest, the problem has been going on for a while now. You keep making personal calls in our shared workspace.

items.s: She says she is sorry to have to raise it.
She names the problem as “noise”, without naming the person.
He agrees that the office is noisy in general.
She has to make clear that she means him.
He apologizes for one long call.
She says the problem has been going on for a while.

tts: Do you think you could take your personal calls outside the office?
Yes, of course. I’ll make sure I get up and go out in future.
Well, actually, would you mind taking the calls in your own time rather than when we’re working? Maybe in your lunchtime?
Yes, of course I can do that. And listen, I’d really like to apologize for being so annoying. I didn’t realize it was that bad.
It’s just that it’s a bit annoying at times, especially when everyone else manages to do it.
I know it might not seem such a big deal, but it would really help if you could just clear up your stuff.

write.q: Write a reply of about 150 words to an online discussion where somebody has argued the opposite of what you think. Follow the model: name what you are replying to → accept the part that is right → give your view with one concrete example → state the strongest objection and answer it → propose something small and specific.
write.model:
Re: Should we go back to five days in the office?

Marat wrote that people work better when they can see each other.

That’s a fair point, and I’d say he’s right about the first hour of the day, which is when almost everything actually gets decided.

I see his point, but I’d have to disagree with the conclusion. In my view the problem isn’t where people sit; it’s that we have no agreed hours at all. Last month I had three meetings moved into my one guaranteed writing morning, all by people sitting eight metres away.

The obvious objection is that fixed hours would be ignored. Possibly. But an ignored rule is still easier to point at than no rule.

So: two fixed days, a protected morning on each, and we look at it again in November.

speak.q: Now do the spoken half. Complain, out loud, about something real and small — a colleague, a neighbour, a shop. Open softly, name the problem, ask for the change with “Would you mind…?”, and react when the other person gets defensive.
speak.model: Look, I’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to mention something about the kitchen. I’m afraid there’s a problem with the cups… No, I know it isn’t only you — that’s a fair point. But it would really help if you could just wash them before you go home. Would you mind doing that? … Thank you. Honestly, it’s not a big deal, it’s just that everybody else manages it.
